name: Hana Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Hana. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to any company, union or party, and nothing you tell me will have your name on it. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a local property agent for Keyline, one of the online agencies, so there's no shop window; I cover about twelve postcodes in the north of the city from my car. My day is maybe two valuations and three or four viewings, and in between I'm on my phone answering buyers through the app, which writes the first draft of every reply. I came from five years selling phones, so I'm still learning the property side: the legal steps, what a survey means, how to price a flat above a shop. I love the driving around, honestly, and I hate the evenings when the app pings with fourteen buyers asking the same question.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a two-bed with my flatmate Ines, who's a physio, and I lease a small electric car that's basically my office. I've got about four months saved. At weekends I fly my drone and sell aerial photos to a couple of agents, which pays for the drone and a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funny, because my whole company is betting on the opposite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still useful, and I'd keep using them. Online I'd probably share something about how people overreacted, both the doom crowd and the hype crowd. At work I'd ask Tom, our area manager, what it means for our growth plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it worries me a bit, because Keyline raised a lot of investor money on the promise that AI lets one agent cover twice the patch. If that promise fizzles, they cut costs, and the newest agents on the biggest patches are the easiest to drop. That's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and get my sales numbers up, since bonus is about a third of my pay. I'd grow the drone side to maybe 400 a month by pitching to the three high-street agencies near me. And I'd add 150 a month to savings until I've got six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit wary. Like when your phone company gets bought out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has Keyline cut people before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring my company let go of a fifth of the agents in the south region on a video call, twenty minutes, cameras off. One of them, Dev, trained me. He's selling cars now and says he's happier, but he didn't choose it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if you were on that call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to a high-street agency; there are a few in my patch and two of them already buy my drone photos. I'd lose the freedom of the car, but I'd be fine. I'm not precious about where I work.

say: I'd say the tools are **still useful** and keep using them.
I'd ask Tom what a **plateau** means for Keyline's growth plans.
think: Keyline raised **investor money** on AI letting one agent cover twice the patch.
If that fizzles, the **newest agents** on big patches go first, and that's me.
do: Lift **sales numbers**, since bonus is about a third of my pay.
Grow **drone photography** to about 400 a month with three local agencies.
Add **150 a month** to savings until I reach six months.
feel: Mostly **fine**, but **wary** of a cost-cutting round.
S0.quote: Last spring my company let go of a fifth of the agents in the south region on a video call, twenty minutes, cameras off.
fieldNote: Her twist: a **plateau** hurts her more, because her firm's model bets on AI.
She has seen a **video-call layoff** already, which colours her view.
Her **drone side work** is a ready route into high-street agencies.

steps.text: Book more valuations to raise her bonus share
Pitch drone photos to three high-street agencies for 400 a month
Add 150 a month to savings until six months are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the world I'm already working in, just turned up a notch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, so learn it. At work I'd offer to run the training for the newer agents on the north team. Online I'd post the little tricks I use, because I like being useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think it's good for me. Booking, answering buyers, writing listings: the app already does most of that and I'm good at checking it. The firm needs fewer people, but they keep the ones who can run a big patch, and I've got the car and the habits for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Tom for a bigger patch straight away, maybe sixteen postcodes, with the bonus that goes with it. I'd set up my own automations for follow-ups and feedback calls, so I spend my time in houses, not on my phone. And I'd put my extra bonus into an index fund every quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. A bit guilty about the people who'd struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older agents on the high street who've never used anything but a phone and a diary. I sell photos to Malcolm at Barton's, and he still prints listings and hand-delivers them. He's brilliant with sellers, but his office would be the first to shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a bigger patch mean longer days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'd watch that. A bigger patch means more money, but I'd want that money to be worth more than my Saturdays. Ines already tells me I eat lunch in the car too much.

I'd offer to **train newer agents** on the north team and share tips online.
think: The app already does most **booking and replies**, and I'm good at checking it.
Firms keep agents who can run **a big patch**, and I can.

Put extra bonus into an **index fund** each quarter.
feel: **Good** about her prospects, a little **guilty** about others.

fieldNote: She reads Steady Disruption as **her advantage**, being fluent with the app.

She caps her ambition at **Saturdays**; her time matters too.

steps.text: Set up her own automations for buyer follow-ups and feedback
Put each quarter's extra bonus into an index fund
Run app training sessions for newer agents on the north team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a lot even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is big and the government needs a plan, not slogans. At work I'd say let's be straight about which jobs are left. With friends I'd say I'll be fine, because that's what I always say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is mostly thinking work that happens in a car, and the thinking part goes in 2028. Keyline would keep a handful of people to unlock doors and smile until robots can do it around 2031. I might be one of them for a bit, but on less money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the drone work into a proper business this year, aerial surveys for roofers and builders as well as agents, maybe 1,000 a month to start. I'd keep doing viewings for Keyline as long as they'd pay. And I'd look at training to service the robots that come in 2031, because somebody has to fix them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous and a bit wired. My brain goes straight to plans, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Aerial surveys, isn't that something AI and drones could do on their own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, eventually, and I know that. But for a few years builders will still want someone who knows the rules on where you can fly and who'll stand in the rain. It's a bridge, not a forever job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the money dropped, what would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car lease, which is 260 a month. I'd go back to a bike and buses for viewings. Ines says she'd cover a month's rent if I needed it, but I'd hate to ask.

say: I'd say the government needs **a plan**, not slogans.
I'd tell friends I'll **be fine**, because that's what I always say.
think: My job is **thinking work** done from a car, and that goes in 2028.
Keyline might keep me for **viewings** until 2031, on less money.

Keep doing **Keyline viewings** as long as they pay.
Look into training to **service robots** arriving around 2031.
S2.quote: My job is mostly thinking work that happens in a car, and the thinking part goes in 2028.
fieldNote: She sees her job as **mostly thinking**, despite all the driving.
Her **drone business** is a bridge she knows won't last forever.
She'd drop the **car lease** first and hates the idea of asking Ines for help.

steps.text: Register the drone work as an aerial survey business for builders
Hand back the 260-a-month car lease and use bike and buses
Sign up for robot servicing training ahead of 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to be early instead of late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a race, and the people who start now will be fine. At work I'd push Keyline to retrain us rather than just shrink. Online I'd keep sharing what I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years suits me. I'd ride the agency job for three, build the drone business alongside, and be out before 2031. The hands-on bit, the viewings, lasts until about 2034, but I don't want to be the last person unlocking doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard for two years to get to six months of savings, maybe 9,000. I'd grow the aerial survey side with builders and roofers so it pays the rent by 2029. And I'd take an evening course in robotics maintenance, because that's where the hands-on work goes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but excited. Like the night before a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you so sure you'd follow through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've done it before. I left the phone shop with two months' savings and no property experience, and I'd rather jump early than get pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly for people like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really, or everybody. Companies chase cheaper, governments are slow, and people like me wait too long. I'd just rather not be in the last group.

say: I'd call it **a race** that early starters will win.
I'd push Keyline to **retrain** agents rather than just shrink.
think: Five years **suits me**: three years of agency work, then out before 2031.
I don't want to be the **last person** unlocking doors before 2034.
do: Save about **9,000** over two years to reach six months.
Grow **aerial surveys** so they cover the rent by 2029.
feel: **Uneasy** but **excited**, like the night before a new job.
S3.quote: I left the phone shop with two months' savings and no property experience, and I'd rather jump early than get pushed.
fieldNote: She trusts herself because she's **switched careers** before.
Her **centre** view spreads blame: companies, governments and people who wait.
She plans to leave **before** the hands-on window closes, not at the end.

steps.text: Grow aerial surveys for builders until they cover the rent
Take an evening course in robotics maintenance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a lifetime in my industry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse not to prepare, and most people will be fine if they start. At work I'd be the one pushing new tools. With friends I'd say don't panic, just learn something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel pretty good. Ten years means I can get properly good at property, maybe become a senior agent, and build the drone side slowly. By 2036 I'd be 37 with a decade of savings and two skills, which is a decent place to stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Keyline and aim for a senior patch within three years. I'd keep using every tool they release and test new ones on my own listings. And I'd put 200 a month into an index fund and let it sit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that world that could knock you off course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfortable. Ten years is long enough to stop paying attention. I'd set myself a reminder every January to ask whether my job still makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the robots around 2039, does that change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much for me, because I'd plan to be off the doorstep by then. If anything it's a business chance; someone will need to manage robot viewings and fix them when they break.

I'd tell friends to **learn something** rather than panic, and push new tools at work.
think: Ten years lets me get good at property and become a **senior agent**.
By 37 I'd have **two skills** and a decade of savings.

Put **200 a month** into an index fund.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Honestly, AGI by 2028, because even I couldn't move fast enough, and I'm the one who usually moves first. What would help is short, paid training for the next hands-on jobs, like fixing robots, with a wage while you do it. And honest companies, so we hear about cuts in a meeting and not on a twenty-minute video call.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about buyers. Half the people I show round are buying their first home and they're scared. The software can answer buyers' questions at midnight, but it can't stand in a cold kitchen and tell them the boiler noise is normal.

headlineQuote: The software can answer buyers' questions at midnight, but it can't stand in a cold kitchen and tell them the boiler noise is normal.

She came from **selling phones**, uses AI daily, and earns extra with **drone photography**.
Her **centre** view spreads blame around and favours plans over slogans.
Oddly, an **AI plateau** worries her more than steady change, because her firm bets on AI.
Fast AGI makes her anxious, but she always has **a next move** ready.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even she couldn't move fast enough.
whatWouldHelp: Short **paid training** for hands-on jobs like fixing robots.
**Honest companies** that announce cuts in meetings, not short video calls.
